claim: CRC is the third most common cancer worldwide and the third leading cause of cancer-related deaths in Western countries.
source: CRC is the third most common cancer worldwide and the third leading cause of cancer-related deaths in Western countries (Malvezzi et al., 2014; Hori et al., 2015; Jemal et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Malvezzi et al., 2014; Hori et al., 2015; Jemal et al., 2017).

claim: Endoscopic removal of adenomatous polyps can reduce CRC-related mortality by more than 50%.
source: It is estimated that the endoscopic removal of adenomatous polyps can reduce CRC-related mortality by more than 50%.
evidence: The claim is stated as an estimate in the manuscript text.

claim: ESD alone is an effective option for T1 CRC patients who are at low risk for developing LNM.
source: Evidence suggests that ESD (endoscopic submucosal dissection) alone is an effective option for T1 CRC patients, who are at low risk for developing LNM, while more extensive radical surgery after ESD is needed for only high-risk patients (Ikematsu et al., 2013; Yoda et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Ikematsu et al., 2013; Yoda et al., 2013).

claim: Approximately 70 to 80% of T1 CRC patients are classified as high risk according to current clinical treatment guidelines.
source: According to the current clinical treatment guidelines, which rely on a histopathological examination, approximately 70 to 80% of patients are classified as high risk (poor tumor differentiation, lymphatic/vascular invasion, and depth of submucosal invasion >1000 mm).
evidence: The claim is stated in the manuscript text describing current clinical guidelines.

claim: Only 8 to 16% of T1 CRC patients' LN status can be accurately predicted by current histopathological guidelines.
source: However, the LN status of only 8 to 16% of patients can be accurately predicted by these guidelines; thus, a large number of LNM-negative patients routinely undergo unnecessary additional surgeries, with an associated postoperative mortality rate of 3–6% (Tanaka et al., 1995; Kobayashi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Tanaka et al., 1995; Kobayashi et al., 2011).

claim: Additional surgery after ESD for T1 CRC has an associated postoperative mortality rate of 3–6%.
source: However, the LN status of only 8 to 16% of patients can be accurately predicted by these guidelines; thus, a large number of LNM-negative patients routinely undergo unnecessary additional surgeries, with an associated postoperative mortality rate of 3–6% (Tanaka et al., 1995; Kobayashi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Tanaka et al., 1995; Kobayashi et al., 2011).

claim: Ozawa et al. developed a predictive model for T1 and T2 CRC using miRNA expression data that achieved an AUC of 0.74.
source: Previously, Ozawa et al., and Kandimalla et al., used the microRNA (miRNA) and messenger RNA (mRNA) expression dataset of T1 and T2 CRC patients from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) as the training cohort to build predictive models, achieved an area under the ROC curve (AUC) values of 0.74 and 0.84, respectively (Ozawa et al., 2018; Kandimalla et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ozawa et al., 2018.

claim: Kandimalla et al. developed a predictive model for T1 and T2 CRC using mRNA expression data that achieved an AUC of 0.84.
source: Previously, Ozawa et al., and Kandimalla et al., used the microRNA (miRNA) and messenger RNA (mRNA) expression dataset of T1 and T2 CRC patients from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) as the training cohort to build predictive models, achieved an area under the ROC curve (AUC) values of 0.74 and 0.84, respectively (Ozawa et al., 2018; Kandimalla et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kandimalla et al., 2019.

claim: Kudo et al. developed an algorithm to predict LNM in 4073 patients with T1 CRC by clinicopathological characteristics and achieved an AUC of 0.83.
source: Most recently, Kudo et al., developed an algorithm to predict LNM in 4073 patients with T1 CRC by clinicopathological characteristics and achieved an AUC of 0.83 (Kudo et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kudo et al., 2021.

claim: The study analyzed FFPE tumor samples from 143 LNM-negative and 78 LNM-positive patients with T1 CRC, totaling 221 individuals.
source: To identify LNM mechanisms and protein signatures for T1NxM0 CRC, we performed mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics to analyze FFPE tumor samples from 143 LNM-negative and 78 LNM-positive patients with T1 CRC, totaling 221 individuals.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the manuscript text describing the study cohort.

claim: LNM in T1 CRC is significantly associated with submucosal invasion depth (p=0.014).
source: As previously reported in T1NxM0 CRC, LNM is significantly associated with the submucosal invasion depth (p=0.014, chi-square test), lymphatic or vascular invasion (p<0.001, chi-square test), and poor differentiation (p=0.004, chi-square test) (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (chi-square test) with p=0.014.

claim: LNM in T1 CRC is significantly associated with lymphatic or vascular invasion (p<0.001).
source: As previously reported in T1NxM0 CRC, LNM is significantly associated with the submucosal invasion depth (p=0.014, chi-square test), lymphatic or vascular invasion (p<0.001, chi-square test), and poor differentiation (p=0.004, chi-square test) (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (chi-square test) with p<0.001.

claim: LNM in T1 CRC is significantly associated with poor differentiation (p=0.004).
source: As previously reported in T1NxM0 CRC, LNM is significantly associated with the submucosal invasion depth (p=0.014, chi-square test), lymphatic or vascular invasion (p<0.001, chi-square test), and poor differentiation (p=0.004, chi-square test) (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (chi-square test) with p=0.004.

claim: Left-sided T1 CRC tumors showed a higher metastatic tendency (41.1% LNM rate) than right-sided tumors (22.0% LNM rate) (p=0.036).
source: In our cohort, the rate of LNM was related to tumor location, specifically. The left-sided tumors (LNM rate: 41.1%) showed a higher metastatic tendency than right-sided (LNM rate: 22.0%) (p=0.036, chi-square test) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (chi-square test) with p=0.036.

claim: 7% of T1 CRC patients in the study cohort were MSI-H.
source: Of the 172 patients for whom MSI status was available, 12 (7%) were MSI-H, which is consistent with previous reported on metastatic CRC by Federico et al., (6.6%) (Innocenti et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the manuscript text and supported by comparison to a cited study.

claim: 16.7% of MSI-H T1 CRC patients had LNM, compared to 39.6% of MSS patients.
source: For MSI-H patients, there were 16.7% (2 of 12) had LNM, and 39.6% (63 of 159) for MSS patients, the MSS group showed a higher tendency of LNM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: More than 13,000 protein groups were identified in the study with a 1% false discovery rate at the peptide and protein levels.
source: Overall, we produced a high-quality dataset (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), more than 13,000 protein groups (with a 1% false discovery rate [FDR] at the peptide and protein levels) were identified, and the identification number of each sample was over 4000 proteins (Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the manuscript text describing the proteomic data quality.

claim: Among 44 reported CRC LNM markers, only CTSD, GSTM3, and MX1 were differentially expressed between LNM-negative and LNM-positive patients in the proteomic data (p<0.05).
source: Among the 44 reported gene or RNA markers, only CTSD, GSTM3, and MX1 (Oh-e et al., 2001; Meding et al., 2012; Croner et al., 2014) were differentially expressed between LNM-negative and LNM-positive patients in our proteomic data (p<0.05, Wilcoxon rank-sum tests) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Wilcoxon rank-sum tests) and references to Figure 2A, with citations to three studies.

claim: 2577 proteins were detected specifically in the T1 CRC cohort compared to previous all-stage CRC proteomic studies.
source: We also compared our data with those of the previous all stage CRC proteomic studies (CPTAC cohort and mCRC cohort) (Zhang et al., 2014; Li et al., 2020b), 4634 proteins were found in all three cohorts, whereas 2577 proteins were detected specifically in our T1 CRC cohort (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with published datasets and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 82 proteins were significantly differentially expressed in LNM-negative T1 CRC patients (identified in at least 30% of samples with log2FC>1 or <-1 and p<0.05).
source: We found that 82 and 84 proteins were significantly differentially expressed in LNM-negative and LNM-positive patients, respectively (identified in at least 30% of samples with a log2-fold change [log2FC]>1 or <-1 and p<0.05, Wilcoxon rank-sum test) (Figure 2B and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Wilcoxon rank-sum test) and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: 84 proteins were significantly differentially expressed in LNM-positive T1 CRC patients (identified in at least 30% of samples with log2FC>1 or <-1 and p<0.05).
source: We found that 82 and 84 proteins were significantly differentially expressed in LNM-negative and LNM-positive patients, respectively (identified in at least 30% of samples with a log2-fold change [log2FC]>1 or <-1 and p<0.05, Wilcoxon rank-sum test) (Figure 2B and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Wilcoxon rank-sum test) and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: 19 FDA-approved drug targets were identified among proteins overrepresented in LNM-positive T1 CRC patients, including F13A1, GBA, GNG2, GUCY1B3, STK3, STK4, and VWF.
source: To search for druggable targets in LNM-positive T1 CRC, we investigated 84 proteins that were overrepresented in LNM-positive patients and identified 19 US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved drug targets: F13A1, GBA, GNG2, GUCY1B3, STK3, STK4, VWF, etc. (Figure 2C and Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of druggable proteins and reference to Figure 2C.

claim: 34 proteins were identified as potential drug targets in LNM-positive T1 CRC patients, including ATAD2, BAIAP2, CEACAM6, FARS2, MX2, OSBPL5, SERPINB5, SERPINB8, SHC1, UBE2Z, YAP1, and ZG16.
source: Furthermore, 34 of these proteins, including ATAD2, BAIAP2, CEACAM6, FARS2, MX2, OSBPL5, SERPINB5, SERPINB8, SHC1, UBE2Z, YAP1, and ZG16, etc. were identified as potential drug targets (Figure 2C; Freshour et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis using the Drug Gene Interaction Database and citation to Freshour et al., 2021.

claim: The epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) pathway was significantly enriched (adjusted p-value <0.05) in the LNM-positive group.
source: The results revealed that only the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) pathway was significantly enriched (adjusted p-value <0.05) in the LNM-positive group, while no significantly enriched pathways in the LNM-negative group (Figure 2D, Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) with adjusted p-value <0.05 and reference to Figure 2D.

claim: Six EMT-related proteins showed significant upregulation (log2FC >1) in LNM-positive T1 CRC patients, including CAP2, PLOD1, and SERPINE2.
source: We also examined the expression of EMT-related proteins and found that all of them were up-regulated in the LNM-positive group compared to the LNM-negative group (log2FC >0; p<0.05, Wilcoxon rank-sum tests), with six proteins showing a significant upregulation (log2FC >1), including CAP2, PLOD1, SERPINE2, etc. (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Wilcoxon rank-sum tests) and reference to Figure 2E.

claim: EMT markers SERPINE2 and LRP1 were significantly upregulated in both the T1 CRC cohort and early-stage CRC group from the mCRC cohort (log2FC >1 and p<0.05).
source: However, when we focused on the early-stage (T1/T2) CRC individuals from the mCRC cohort and compared the EMT marker expression between the LNM-positive and LNM-negative groups, the EMT markers like SERPINE2 and LRP1 were significantly upregulated in both our cohort and the early-stage CRC group from the mCRC cohort (log2FC >1 and p<0.05, Wilcoxon rank-sum test) (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Wilcoxon rank-sum test) and reference to Figures 2F and G.

claim: Cytoskeletal remodeling proteins including ABI1, SPTA1, SPTB, ANK1, MRPL46, and ITGA2B were down-regulated in LNM-positive T1 CRC patients (log2FC <-1 and p<0.05).
source: Cytoskeletal remodeling proteins, including ABI1, SPTA1, SPTB, ANK1, MRPL46, and ITGA2B were down-regulated in patients with LNM compared with those without LNM (log2FC <-1 and p<0.05, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Wilcoxon rank-sum test).

claim: Amino acid metabolism pathways including 'valine, leucine, and isoleucine degradation' and 'glycine, serine, and threonine metabolism' were enriched in the LNM-negative group (adjusted p≤0.05).
source: Amino acid metabolism pathways, such as 'valine, leucine, and isoleucine degradation' (hsa00280) and 'glycine, serine, and threonine metabolism' (hsa00260), were found to be enriched in the LNM-negative group (adjusted p≤0.05, limma approach), and related proteins (TMLHE, SLC44A2, SHMT1, and EEF1E1) were up-regulated in the LNM-negative group (Log2FC <1, p<0.05) (Figure 2K).
evidence: The claim is supported by ssGSEA analysis with adjusted p≤0.05 and reference to Figure 2K.

claim: Lipid metabolism pathways including 'arachidonic acid metabolism' and 'steroid biosynthesis' were enriched in the LNM-positive group.
source: On the other hand, the LNM-positive group mainly expressed lipid metabolism pathways, such as 'arachidonic acid metabolism' (hsa00590) and 'steroid biosynthesis' (hsa00100), which are known to promote cancer cell proliferation and migration and are involved in the regulation of EMT.
evidence: The claim is supported by pathway enrichment analysis.

claim: The LNM-positive group was significantly enriched in coagulation cascades.
source: Interestingly, the LNM-positive group was significantly enriched in coagulation cascades (Figure 2L), which occurred during EMT, and previous studies have indicated that the inhibition of coagulation greatly limits cancer metastasis (Gil-Bernabé et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by pathway enrichment analysis, reference to Figure 2L, and citation to Gil-Bernabé et al., 2013.

claim: Twelve proteins related to coagulation cascades were elevated in LNM-positive T1 CRC patients (log2FC >1 and p<0.05).
source: Twelve of the 84 proteins that were elevated in LNM-positive patients (log2FC >1 and p<0.05, Wilcoxon rank-sum test) were related to coagulation cascades (Figure 2M), and many of these 12 proteins are known or suspected to be linked to CRC or other cancer metastasis.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Wilcoxon rank-sum test) and reference to Figure 2M.

claim: The ratio of LNM was significantly higher in poorly differentiated T1 CRC patients (48.6%) compared with well-moderately differentiated patients (28.8%) (p=0.004).
source: In agreement with previous reports (Ikematsu et al., 2013), in our T1 CRC cohort the ratio of LNM was significantly higher in patients with poorly poor differentiated patients (48.6%) compared with well-moderately differentiated patients, in T1 CRC (28.8%) (p=0.004, chi-square test), Mucinous adenocarcinoma patients (55%) also shown a greater tendency to LNM than adenocarcinoma (30.1%) (p=0.004, chi-square test) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), and mucinous adenocarcinoma was considered to be a significant risk factor of LNM in T1 CRC (Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (chi-square test) with p=0.004 and citation to Ikematsu et al., 2013.

claim: Mucinous adenocarcinoma patients showed a greater tendency to LNM (55%) than adenocarcinoma patients (30.1%) (p=0.004).
source: In agreement with previous reports (Ikematsu et al., 2013), in our T1 CRC cohort the ratio of LNM was significantly higher in patients with poorly poor differentiated patients (48.6%) compared with well-moderately differentiated patients, in T1 CRC (28.8%) (p=0.004, chi-square test), Mucinous adenocarcinoma patients (55%) also shown a greater tendency to LNM than adenocarcinoma (30.1%) (p=0.004, chi-square test) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), and mucinous adenocarcinoma was considered to be a significant risk factor of LNM in T1 CRC (Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (chi-square test) with p=0.004 and citation to Xu et al., 2020.

claim: 140 proteins were overexpressed in well to moderately-differentiated adenocarcinoma (log2FC >1, p<0.05).
source: As a result, 140 proteins were overexpressed in DS1(log2FC >1, mean of DS1 vs mean of DS2 and DS3; p<0.05, Kruskal-Walli's test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Kruskal-Walli's test) with p<0.05.

claim: Oxidative phosphorylation and TCA cycle pathways were higher in well to moderately-differentiated adenocarcinoma than in poorly differentiated and mucinous adenocarcinoma (p<0.05).
source: Further pathway enrichment analysis revealed that the oxidative phosphorylation and TCA cycle pathways were higher in DS1 than in DS2 and DS3 (p<0.05) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by pathway enrichment analysis with p<0.05 and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: 178 proteins were highly expressed in poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma (log2FC >1, p<0.05) and enriched in GTPase activity and Wnt signaling pathways.
source: In DS2, 178 proteins were highly expressed (log2FC >1, mean of DS2 vs mean of DS1 and DS3; p<0.05, Kruskal-Walli's test) and enriched in the GTPase activity and Wnt signaling pathways.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Kruskal-Walli's test) with p<0.05 and pathway enrichment analysis.

claim: 326 proteins were overexpressed in mucinous adenocarcinoma (log2FC >1, p<0.05), functioning in ECM organization, cell migration, and vesicle-mediated transport.
source: In DS3, 326 proteins were overexpressed (log2FC >1, mean of DS3 vs mean of DS1 and DS2; p<0.05, Kruskal-Walli's test), functioning in more aggressive pathways such as ECM organization, cell migration, and vesicle-mediated transport.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Kruskal-Walli's test) with p<0.05 and pathway enrichment analysis.

claim: Six integrins (ITGA1, ITGAV, ITGA11, ITGA9, ITGB3, and ITGB5) were overexpressed in mucinous adenocarcinoma.
source: We found that six integrins (ITGA1, ITGAV, ITGA11, ITGA9, ITGB3, and ITGB5) and 11 reported extracellular vesicle (EV) markers (ADIRF, CSPG4, DPP4, ENTPD1, LRG1, PECAM1, PLVAP, RAB25, TMEM2, TTR, and YBX1) were overexpressed in the mucinous adenocarcinoma group (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F, G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2F.

claim: 11 extracellular vesicle markers (ADIRF, CSPG4, DPP4, ENTPD1, LRG1, PECAM1, PLVAP, RAB25, TMEM2, TTR, and YBX1) were overexpressed in mucinous adenocarcinoma.
source: We found that six integrins (ITGA1, ITGAV, ITGA11, ITGA9, ITGB3, and ITGB5) and 11 reported extracellular vesicle (EV) markers (ADIRF, CSPG4, DPP4, ENTPD1, LRG1, PECAM1, PLVAP, RAB25, TMEM2, TTR, and YBX1) were overexpressed in the mucinous adenocarcinoma group (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F, G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2G.

claim: The stromal score was significantly higher in mucinous colorectal adenocarcinoma than in non-mucinous adenocarcinoma (p<0.05).
source: The stromal score was significantly higher in mucinous colorectal adenocarcinoma than in non-mucinous adenocarcinoma (p<0.05, Kruskal-Wallis test), and the signatures of endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells, and osteoblasts were enriched in mucinous colorectal adenocarcinoma; however, pericytes were decreased.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Kruskal-Wallis test) with p<0.05.

claim: D2-40 expression in mucinous adenocarcinoma was significantly higher than in non-mucinous adenocarcinoma.
source: Immunostaining showed the D2-40 expression in mucinous adenocarcinoma was significantly higher than that in non-mucinous adenocarcinoma, in agreement with the proteomics data (Figure 2—figure supplement 2J and Figure 2—source data 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2J.

claim: A 55-protein classifier achieved an AUC of 1.00 (95% CI, 1.000) in the training cohort through 10-fold cross-validation.
source: The classifier achieved an AUC of 1.00 (95% CI, 1.000) through 10-fold cross-validation in the training cohort, which indicated higher predictive power for LNM than the NCCN guidelines (AUC = 0.561) (p<0.001) (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis with 10-fold cross-validation and reference to Figure 3B.

claim: The 55-protein classifier yielded 100% sensitivity and specificity in the training cohort.
source: The Youden's index-derived cutoff was used as the threshold, and the 55-protein classifier yielded 100% sensitivity and specificity, whereas the NCCN guidelines yielded 93.5% sensitivity and 18.6% specificity.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis using Youden's index.

claim: The 55-protein classifier achieved an AUC of 0.96 (95% CI, 0.917–1.000) in validation cohort 1 (ESD cohort).
source: The 55-protein classifier achieved an AUC of 0.96 (95% CI, 0.917–1.000) in distinguishing LNM-positive from LNM-negative patients with 100% sensitivity/94.3% specificity in VC1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 3C.

claim: The 55-protein classifier achieved an AUC of 0.93 in validation cohort 2 (prospective cohort) with 88.9% sensitivity and 84.2% specificity.
source: The classifier based on the intensities of the 55 proteins achieved 88.9% sensitivity and 84.2% specificity in distinguishing LNM-negative and LNM-positive T1 CRC patients, with an AUC of 0.93 (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 3D.

claim: Using NCCN guidelines, 88% of patients (195 of 221) were stratified into high-risk category, but only 37% (73 of 195) were actually high risk.
source: When we used current clinical treatment guidelines (NCCN guidelines), it resulted in stratifying 88% patients (195 of the 221) into a high-risk category and the remaining 12% (26 of 195) into a low-risk group, only 37% (73 of 195) of patients are actually high risk, 63% (122 of 195) of patients underwent unnecessary additional surgery, and there are five (9.2%, 5 of 26) LNM-positive cases mistakenly assigned to the low-risk group (Figure 3E and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis and reference to Figure 3E.

claim: Using the 55-protein classifier, 72% (78 of 107) of high-risk patients had LNM, indicating only 27.1% (29 of 107) were overtreated.
source: In contrast, of the 107 patients who are classified as high risk by our model, 78 had LNM (72%), indicating that only 27.1% (29 of 107) of all patients with T1 CRC were overtreated, and all the patients stratified into the low-risk group are LNM-negative (Figure 3E and Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis and reference to Figure 3E.

claim: A simplified 9-protein classifier achieved an AUC of 0.824 (95% CI, 0.767–0.881) after bootstrapping with 1000 resamples.
source: After using bootstraps with 1000 resamples for validation, the AUC of the simplified model was 0.824 (95% CI, 0.767–0.881) (Figure 3F), and the calibration curve demonstrated good agreement between the predicted status and the true status, with an error of 0.021 (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis with bootstrapping and reference to Figure 3F.

claim: The 9-protein simplified classifier showed 100% sensitivity and 70% specificity in the mCRC cohort (T1/2 CRC patients).
source: In mCRC cohort (T1/2 CRC patients, N=16; LNM−, N=13; LNM+, N=3), nine LNM-negative patients were classified into the low-risk group, and all the patients stratified into the low-risk group are LNM-negative, corresponding to a sensitivity of 100% and a specificity of 70% (Figure 3I).
evidence: The claim is supported by external validation data and reference to Figure 3I.

claim: The 9-protein simplified classifier showed 100% sensitivity and 73% specificity in the CPTAC cohort (T1/2 CRC patients).
source: In the CPTAC cohort (T1/2 CRC patients, N=16; LNM-, N=15; LNM+, N=1), 11 out of 15 LNM-negative patients were correctly identified, corresponding to a specificity of 73%. Although, the results were limited by the number of LNM-positive patients, LNM-positive patients were successfully assigned to the high-risk group with a sensitivity of 100% (Figure 3J).
evidence: The claim is supported by external validation data and reference to Figure 3J.

claim: IHC staining of ABI1 showed an overall increase in LNM-negative patients (p=0.007).
source: In agreement with the proteomics data, staining of ABI1 (p=0.007), ITPR2 (p=0.054), and RHOT2 (p=0.011) showed an overall increase in LNM-negative patients (Figure 4A and B, Student's t-test), whereas ATAD2 (p=0.034) and ISLR (p=0.044) showed an overall increase in LNM-positive patients (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, Student's t-test) according to the proteomics data.
evidence: The claim is supported by IHC data with statistical analysis (Student's t-test) and reference to Figure 4A.

claim: IHC staining of RHOT2 showed an overall increase in LNM-negative patients (p=0.011).
source: In agreement with the proteomics data, staining of ABI1 (p=0.007), ITPR2 (p=0.054), and RHOT2 (p=0.011) showed an overall increase in LNM-negative patients (Figure 4A and B, Student's t-test), whereas ATAD2 (p=0.034) and ISLR (p=0.044) showed an overall increase in LNM-positive patients (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, Student's t-test) according to the proteomics data.
evidence: The claim is supported by IHC data with statistical analysis (Student's t-test) and reference to Figure 4A.

claim: IHC staining of ATAD2 showed an overall increase in LNM-positive patients (p=0.034).
source: In agreement with the proteomics data, staining of ABI1 (p=0.007), ITPR2 (p=0.054), and RHOT2 (p=0.011) showed an overall increase in LNM-negative patients (Figure 4A and B, Student's t-test), whereas ATAD2 (p=0.034) and ISLR (p=0.044) showed an overall increase in LNM-positive patients (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, Student's t-test) according to the proteomics data.
evidence: The claim is supported by IHC data with statistical analysis (Student's t-test) and reference to Figure 4A.

claim: IHC staining of ISLR showed an overall increase in LNM-positive patients (p=0.044).
source: In agreement with the proteomics data, staining of ABI1 (p=0.007), ITPR2 (p=0.054), and RHOT2 (p=0.011) showed an overall increase in LNM-negative patients (Figure 4A and B, Student's t-test), whereas ATAD2 (p=0.034) and ISLR (p=0.044) showed an overall increase in LNM-positive patients (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, Student's t-test) according to the proteomics data.
evidence: The claim is supported by IHC data with statistical analysis (Student's t-test) and reference to Figure 4A.

claim: A 5-protein IHC classifier achieved an AUC of 0.825 in 47 patients.
source: Using binary logistic regression to analyze the results of these proteins, we obtained a 5-protein classifier using the IHC score. The 5-protein IHC classifier achieved an AUC of 0.825 in 47 patients (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis using binary logistic regression and reference to Figure 4B.

claim: RHOT2 was significantly down-regulated (Log2FC = −1.35; p=0.003) in LNM-positive patients compared with LNM-negative patients.
source: RHOT2 was significantly down-regulated (Log2FC = −1.35; p=0.003, Wilcoxon rank-sum test) in LNM-positive patients compared with LNM-negative patients in our T1 CRC cohort.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Wilcoxon rank-sum test) with p=0.003.

claim: Low level of RHOT2 is related to low overall survival of patients with colon cancer (p<0.05).
source: Furthermore, as shown in Figure 4C, the analysis on the basis of the TCGA database suggested that the low level of RHOT2 is related to the low overall survival of patients with colon cancer (Figure 4C, p<0.05) (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival analysis using TCGA data with p<0.05 and citation to Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: 1508 proteins were correlated significantly (p<0.05) with RHOT2, with 1354 showing positive correlation and 154 showing negative correlation.
source: We found 1508 proteins were correlated significantly (p<0.05, Spearman) with RHOT2, and 1354 proteins showed a positive correlation (coefficient >0) with RHOT2, 154 proteins were negatively correlated with RHOT2 (coefficient <0) (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis (Spearman) with p<0.05 and reference to Figure 4D.

claim: RHOT2 silence significantly enhanced migration and invasion of colon cancer cells (p<0.05).
source: The results of the transwell assay showed that the migration ability of colon cancer cells was significantly increased by si-RHOT2 (Figure 4H, I, Student's t-test,p<0.05). Low expression level of RHOT2 markedly enhanced the migration ability of colon cancer cells (p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by transwell assay data with statistical analysis (Student's t-test) and reference to Figures 4H and I.
